record.paper_title: Open problems in ageing science: A roadmap for biogerontology
record.original_question: Which ageing-related changes observed in model organisms also occur in a similar way in humans?

evidence.quote: Which ageing changes in model organisms also change in a similar way in humans?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Identify and characterize which ageing-associated biological changes documented in standard laboratory model organisms (such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and Mus musculus) occur in humans in a qualitatively and quantitatively similar manner. Specifically: (i) enumerate the cellular, molecular, physiological, and organismal changes that accompany ageing in each model organism; (ii) for each such change, determine whether an analogous change is observed during human ageing, and specify the criteria (e.g., shared molecular pathway, comparable kinetics, comparable phenotypic consequence) under which the two are deemed "similar"; (iii) classify the changes into those that are conserved across species, those that are model-specific, and those whose conservation status is currently undetermined.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an open biological research question rather than a mathematical problem. The comparison of ageing-related changes between model organisms and humans is an active area of biogerontology research; while certain hallmarks of ageing (e.g., genomic instability, telomere attrition, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction) are widely regarded as conserved, a comprehensive and validated mapping remains incomplete and is the subject of ongoing investigation.

status_evidence.title: The Hallmarks of Aging
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies nine candidate hallmarks of ageing thought to be largely conserved across mammals including humans.
status_evidence.claim: Several ageing changes seen in model organisms are believed to be conserved in humans, but the mapping is incomplete.
